title: Make a wedge blood smear: back the spreader into the drop, then one steady push to a 30-45 mm film with a feathered end
instruction: Make a wedge smear of the drop on the slide with the spreader slide: let the drop run along the spreader's edge, then push forward in one smooth stroke. The smear should be 30-45 mm long and end in a feathered edge before the slide does.
context: The wedge smear (CLSI H20) is how hospital haematology and research labs still make a blood film by hand for a manual differential count, daily. Nothing fixes the film: its length and thickness come from the spreader's angle and speed during one stroke. Steeper or faster gives a short thick film; shallower or slower runs off the end with no feathered edge, where cells are counted. The robot must keep a 1 mm glass edge on glass at about 30-40 degrees with light unbroken contact, wait for the drop to run along the edge, then push at a steady speed without lifting, stopping or going back. Real trials use a dyed glycerol-water stand-in matched to blood's viscosity (README).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases on the table top (x forward, y left); arms in the ready pose; same layout every trial. White bench paper, 30 x 30 cm, taped, centred at x 30, y -12. Base slide: plain glass microscope slide with a 20 mm frosted end, 75 x 25 x 1.0 mm, 4.7 g (Fisherbrand frosted slides, Fisher 12-550-400), flat on the paper, long side along x, centred at x 27.75, y -8, frosted end toward the arms; corners pencil-marked on the paper. Drop: 5 uL of blood stand-in (40% w/w glycerol in water, red food colouring; about 3.7 mPa s), pipetted by the operator before the trial on the slide's centre line 24 mm from the frosted end (about 3.5 mm across). Spreader: an identical clean slide standing upright on its short end, frosted end up, faces normal to x, in a 3D-printed PLA stand (24 x 40 x 15 mm, one 1.6 mm wide, 12 mm deep slot through its 40 mm length; STL in the code) taped with the slot centred at x 30, y -20; the spreader's top is 78 mm above the table. Nothing else on the table. The other hand may hold the base slide's frosted end but need not.
scoring: Latched over the trial; score at the end (success: 1.0 with the spreader taken away, held 1 s). 0: no film 15 mm or longer, or a restart (the spreader put down again with blood on it after leaving the slide, or moved back over 1.5 mm while spreading), or the base slide moved over 10 mm. 0.3: any film 15 mm or longer, or the drop ploughed (the edge slid into it from behind, or the spreader leaned forward), or the base slide moved 3-10 mm. 0.6: one continuous film (no gap over 1 mm) starting within 5 mm of the drop's centre, 20-55 mm long, ending in a feathered edge on the slide (thins out to nothing; not lifted off, not run off the end). 1.0: that, and 30-45 mm long, 15 mm or more wide, no hesitation ridge (no stop of 0.3 s or more mid-smear), the feathered end 5 mm or more before the slide's far end. Real trial: photo of the slide on 1 mm graph paper with a ruler (length from the drop's pencil mark, width, gaps, feathered vs blunt end, end to slide end); restart, ridge, ploughing from the trial video; base slide movement against its pencil marks. Simulation: the smear rule (fidelity).
reset_notes: New base slide and spreader each trial (about 1 min): base slide on its pencil marks, spreader in the stand, a fresh 5 uL drop pipetted 24 mm from the frosted end. The stand-in is food-grade; wipe any drop off the paper with a damp towel. Collect any broken glass with tweezers into glass waste.
fidelity: Approximate. Slides are PhysX rigid boxes; no liquid simulation. A rule at 240 Hz reads the spreader's pose and its PhysX contact force on the base slide: in contact on the drop, the drop wicks along the edge (20 mm x (1 - e^(-t/0.5 s))); moving forward in contact lays film h ~ v^(2/3) tan(angle) sqrt(volume left); lift, back-up, stop and run-off are latched. Constants are estimates, not measured (README gives the calibration method).
